collins.hedgehog: None. Collins's comparison company started in a position similar to Pitney Bowes (an entrenched office-equipment franchise of similar size) but never found what it could be best at. Its later CEO pursued a grand vision of dominating office automation against far stronger rivals, and the company lurched between strategies.
hedgehog_key_points: should narrow to where it could be best (e.g. quick-print duplicating niches) instead of a grand office-automation vision
collins.stop_doing: Stop chasing leadership in electronic office automation against giants; stop trying to defend every legacy line. Narrow to the niches where it could be best and fund only those.
stop_doing_key_points: do not bet the company on beating IBM/Xerox-class rivals in office automation
exit or shrink lines it cannot lead
collins.leader_type: Not Level 5. Collins cites Roy Ash (CEO from 1976) as a charismatic, high-ego leader with a grand vision to dominate office automation; the bet drained the company and the board pushed him out in 1981.
brutal_facts: growth has stalled since the late 1960s

later_history: Roy Ash became chairman and CEO in September 1976, made deep cuts, moved headquarters from Cleveland to Los Angeles (1978) to project a high-tech image, and renamed the company AM International (1979). Earned only $5.8M on $909.6M of sales in 1980, then posted severe losses. Ash left in 1981; the Addressograph unit was sold in late 1981. Filed for Chapter 11 in April 1982 and closed its Cleveland plant; reorganized in 1984; went bankrupt again in 1993; bought by an investor group in 1996.
notes: Direct comparison company for A17 (Pitney Bowes). Pre-1976 company data is thin on the open web; the dossier uses only what could be sourced and lists the rest as missing.
